class.name: MySQLConfig
class.brief_description: Connection settings for [MySQLSession] and [MySQLPool]: credentials, transport, and behavior toggles.
class.description: Holds everything needed to open a connection: [member host]/[member port] or [member unix_socket_path], [member user]/[member database] and the password (write-only, see [method set_password]), plus [member transport_mode] and a set of limits and behavior toggles below. Meant to be set up once and then treated as immutable: build it, configure it, then pass it to [method MySQLSession.set_config] or [method MySQLPool.set_config]. Changing it afterwards is not supported and can produce inconsistent behavior between connections that already used the old values and ones that have not connected yet. [b]This module talks to a real database over the network and is meant for a headless Godot server or an internal tool, never for a game shipped to players.[/b] Anyone who can reach the exported game can also reach whatever this [MySQLConfig] points to. Use a database user with the minimum privileges the game needs (for example, no [code]DROP[/code]/[code]ALTER[/code] on a user that only ever runs [code]SELECT[/code]/[code]INSERT[/code]), never a database administrator account, and keep [member transport_mode] at [constant TCP_TLS_REQUIRED] (the default) unless you have a specific, trusted reason not to.

method.name: set_password
method.description: Sets the password used by the next [method MySQLSession.connect_db]. Write-only: there is no [code]get_password()[/code], so a script that receives a [MySQLConfig] cannot read the password back out of it. The previous password (if any) is wiped from memory before being replaced.

members.member: If [code]true[/code], negotiates [code]CLIENT_MULTI_STATEMENTS[/code] with the server, so a single [method MySQLSession.execute_text] call may contain several [code];[/code]-separated statements and return several resultsets (see [method MySQLResult.get_resultset_count]). Off by default because it widens the SQL injection surface of any code that builds queries by concatenation. Independent of [member allow_sql_script_execution]. Emits a warning when set to [code]true[/code].

If [code]true[/code], allows [method MySQLSession.execute_script] to run. Off by default for the same reason as [member allow_multi_queries], which it does not imply or depend on. Emits a warning when set to [code]true[/code].

Timeout, in milliseconds, of an asynchronous operation ([method MySQLSession.async_execute_text], [method MySQLSession.async_execute_prepared]). [code]0[/code] means no timeout; a negative value is rejected with an error and the previous value is kept. It is applied per network round trip of the operation (each step of reading the result), not once for the whole call: a result read in several batches or with several resultsets gets a fresh budget on every step instead of one shared deadline for all of them. Has no effect on the synchronous [code]execute_*[/code] methods, which block until the server answers.
Schema selected right after connecting, equivalent to [code]USE[/code].
Server host name or IP address, used when [member transport_mode] is not [constant UNIX_SOCKET]. Ignored otherwise.

How [code]JSON[/code] columns are returned by [method MySQLResult.get_rows]. See [enum JsonResultMode]. Whether this has any effect at all depends on the server: MySQL reports a distinct [code]JSON[/code] column type, but MariaDB does not (it is an alias of [code]LONGTEXT[/code] on the wire), so on MariaDB [constant PARSED_VARIANT] behaves exactly like [constant RAW_STRING].

Limit, in bytes, on the size of a single protocol packet: one request sent, or one row received. This bounds a single row, not the total size of a result (see [member max_result_bytes] for that). Exceeding it fails the call explicitly instead of truncating anything. Must be at least [code]1024[/code] (the size of the buffer every connection starts with); a smaller value is rejected with an error and the previous value is kept.

Limit, in bytes, on the total estimated size of a single [code]execute_*[/code] result (every resultset, every row added up). [code]0[/code] means no limit; a negative value is rejected with an error and the previous value is kept. Unlike [member max_buffer_size], which Boost.MySQL enforces per row after the fact, this is checked while the result is still being read, so a query that would go over the limit is aborted as soon as it does, bounding peak memory instead of only failing once the whole (oversized) result has already been built. The size counted per cell is an estimate (the exact byte length for strings/blobs, a small fixed cost for every other type), not the protocol wire size. Enforced on every [code]execute_*[/code] and [code]async_execute_*[/code] method; [method MySQLSession.execute_streaming] is unaffected, since it already reads the result incrementally and hands control back to the caller between batches.

Server TCP port, used when [member transport_mode] is not [constant UNIX_SOCKET]. Ignored otherwise. Must be between [code]1[/code] and [code]65535[/code]; any other value is rejected with an error and the previous value is kept.

Max number of prepared statements kept per connection by [method MySQLSession.execute_prepared] and [method MySQLSession.async_execute_prepared] (LRU: the least recently used one is closed on the server to make room for a new one). Setting it too high across a pool of many connections can approach the server's [code]max_prepared_stmt_count[/code] system variable, which is a single limit shared by every connection on that server, not a per-connection one.

If [code]true[/code], a [code]TINYINT(1)[/code] column is returned as [bool] instead of [int]. Matches the common convention of using [code]TINYINT(1)[/code] as a boolean column, but is off by default because the module has no way to distinguish that convention from a plain 1-digit integer column at the protocol level; MySQL/MariaDB provide no other signal for this.

How the connection reaches the server. See [enum TransportMode]. Defaults to [constant TCP_TLS_REQUIRED]; setting it to [constant TCP_TLS_DISABLED] emits a warning, since it sends credentials and data unencrypted.

Path to the server's UNIX domain socket, used only when [member transport_mode] is [constant UNIX_SOCKET]. There is no TLS-over-UNIX-socket combination: a local socket is local by nature, so [constant UNIX_SOCKET] always ignores TLS.
Database user name. See the security warning in the class description about using a minimum-privilege user.

constants.constant: Plain TCP, no TLS. Credentials and data travel unencrypted. Setting [member transport_mode] to this value emits a warning.

TCP, using TLS if the server offers it, falling back to plaintext otherwise. Vulnerable to a downgrade attack by anyone who can intercept the connection before it is established; prefer [constant TCP_TLS_REQUIRED] unless you have a specific reason not to.

TCP with TLS required; the connection fails if the server does not offer TLS or its certificate cannot be validated. The default, and the recommended setting for anything that is not a fully trusted local/test network.
A local UNIX domain socket ([member unix_socket_path]) instead of TCP. Never uses TLS (see [member unix_socket_path]); [member host]/[member port] are ignored.
A [code]JSON[/code] column is returned as the raw text [String], never parsed.

A [code]JSON[/code] column is parsed eagerly, as part of building the [MySQLResult], into whatever [method JSON.parse_string] would return (a [Dictionary], [Array], number, [String], [bool] or [code]null[/code]). Only takes effect on a server that reports a distinct [code]JSON[/code] column type (MySQL); on one that does not (MariaDB) this behaves like [constant RAW_STRING].

The default. A [code]JSON[/code] column keeps the raw text in [method MySQLResult.get_rows], exactly like [constant RAW_STRING], and is only parsed (with a cache, so parsing the same cell twice is free the second time) when [method MySQLResult.get_parsed_json] is explicitly called for that cell.
